prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BUZZARDS BAY, Massachusetts (CNN)  -- A crew member aboard a freighter seized by pirates off east  Africa said Wednesday that the crew had captured one of four pirates who hijacked their vessel, but they released him in a failed hostage trade. Shane Murphy is one of the crew members on board the U.S. ship that was hijacked off Somalia's coast. The crew of the U.S.-flagged Maersk Alabama had hoped their release of the pirate would lead the pirates to release Capt. Richard Phillips, but it did not, crew member Ken Quinn told CNN in a satellite telephone call. Instead, the four pirates -- who had scuttled their boat when they boarded the ship armed with AK-47s -- took Phillips with them aboard the ship's 28-foot lifeboat, Quinn said. The crew had earlier overpowered the pirates and forced them off the ship, according to messages from first officer Shane Murphy. Murphy relayed the information in quick phone calls to his wife and father in his home state of Massachusetts -- where his father, Joe Murphy, is a maritime instructor, and his son once lectured about dealing with hostage situations.  Watch Shane Murphy's wife recall the conversation » . Joe Murphy, who teaches at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy, said the crew sent a distress signal to which the U.S. Navy responded immediately from almost 200 miles away. The ship had eluded the pirates for more than three hours off the coast of Somalia before being boarded, Joe Murphy said his son reported. After hiding from their attackers, then leading them to believe they were more in command of the situation than they really were, the crew jumped the pirates, capturing one of them, the elder Murphy said his son told him. "It was by sheer force," he said. "They have no weapons -- it must have been, obviously, that they overpowered them." He said three other pirates "had gone into the water." Pentagon officials confirmed that four hijackers had boarded the Maersk Alabama Wednesday morning, and that one had been in custody. Joe Murphy said his son was in contact with the pirates Wednesday evening, helping negotiate for the release of the captain. He said he can only shake his head at the timing of the attack. Two weeks ago, Shane Murphy visited his father's class to lecture the students on situations like the one he now faces. "This is a classic example of Murphy's law," Joe Murphy said. "I teach the course, my son goes to sea and he gets captured." He said that, despite his concerns, he has faith that his son's experience and knowledge will help wrap up the tense situation. "Hopefully, it's all going to work out," he said. "I think this is going to end as a very positive story." CNN's Jason Carroll and Tom Watkins contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**BUZZARDS BAY, Massachusetts (CNN) —** A crew member aboard a freighter seized by pirates off East Africa said Wednesday that the crew had captured one of the four pirates who hijacked the vessel but later released him in an unsuccessful hostage exchange.

Shane Murphy was among the crew members aboard the U.S. ship hijacked off the coast of Somalia. The crew of the U.S.-flagged *Maersk Alabama* had hoped that releasing the pirate would prompt the other pirates to free Capt. Richard Phillips, but it did not, crew member Ken Quinn told CNN during a satellite phone call.

Instead, the four pirates—who had scuttled their boat after boarding the ship armed with AK-47s—took Phillips with them aboard the ship’s 28-foot lifeboat, Quinn said.

According to messages from first officer Shane Murphy, the crew had earlier overpowered the pirates and forced them off the ship. Murphy relayed the information during brief phone calls to his wife and father in his home state of Massachusetts. His father, Joe Murphy, is a maritime instructor, and his son had once lectured about handling hostage situations.

*Watch Shane Murphy’s wife recall the conversation »*

Joe Murphy, who teaches at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy, said the crew sent a distress signal to which the U.S. Navy responded immediately from nearly 200 miles away.

The ship had evaded the pirates for more than three hours off the coast of Somalia before they boarded, Joe Murphy said his son reported. After hiding from their attackers and then leading them to believe the crew had greater control of the situation than it actually did, the crew ambushed the pirates and captured one of them, the elder Murphy said his son told him.

“It was by sheer force,” he said. “They have no weapons—it must have been, obviously, that they overpowered them.”

He said the three other pirates “had gone into the water.”

Pentagon officials confirmed that four hijackers had boarded the *Maersk Alabama* on Wednesday morning and that one had been taken into custody.

Joe Murphy said his son remained in contact with the pirates Wednesday evening, helping to negotiate the captain’s release. He said he could only shake his head at the timing of the attack.

Two weeks earlier, Shane Murphy had visited his father’s class to lecture students about situations like the one he now faced.

“This is a classic example of Murphy’s law,” Joe Murphy said. “I teach the course, my son goes to sea and he gets captured.”

Despite his concerns, he said he had faith that his son’s experience and knowledge would help bring the tense situation to a close.

“Hopefully, it’s all going to work out,” he said. “I think this is going to end as a very positive story.”

CNN’s Jason Carroll and Tom Watkins contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
**BUZZARDS BAY, Massachusetts (CNN) —** A sailor on a cargo ship attacked by pirates near East Africa said Wednesday that crew members had subdued one of the four hijackers. They later freed the captive pirate in an unsuccessful attempt to exchange him for their captain.

Shane Murphy was among the crew aboard the U.S.-flagged *Maersk Alabama*, which was hijacked off Somalia. In a satellite phone interview with CNN, crewman Ken Quinn said they believed releasing the pirate would persuade the others to free Capt. Richard Phillips. The exchange did not go as planned.

The four gunmen, who were carrying AK-47s and had sunk their own craft after boarding the freighter, instead departed in the ship’s 28-foot lifeboat with Phillips as their hostage, Quinn said.

Messages from first officer Shane Murphy indicated that the crew had previously overwhelmed the hijackers and driven them from the vessel. Murphy shared brief updates by phone with his wife and his father in Massachusetts. His father, Joe Murphy, is an instructor in maritime studies, and Shane had once addressed his class on how to handle hostage crises. A video showed Murphy’s wife describing their conversation.

Joe Murphy, an instructor at the Massachusetts Maritime Academy, said the ship transmitted an emergency alert and that the U.S. Navy responded immediately, despite being nearly 200 miles away.

According to what Shane told his father, the freighter managed to avoid the pirates for more than three hours off Somalia before the attackers succeeded in boarding. The sailors initially concealed themselves, then convinced the gunmen that the crew had greater control of events than was actually the case. They subsequently rushed the pirates and seized one of them.

Joe Murphy said the crew accomplished this entirely through physical force. Because the sailors were unarmed, he explained, they must simply have overpowered the attackers. He added that the remaining three pirates had entered the water.

Pentagon representatives verified that four hijackers boarded the *Maersk Alabama* on Wednesday morning and confirmed that one of them had been detained.

By Wednesday evening, Joe Murphy said, his son was communicating with the pirates and assisting in negotiations aimed at securing the captain’s freedom.

The timing of the incident struck him as especially ironic. Only two weeks earlier, Shane had spoken to students in his father’s class about precisely the kind of emergency he was now experiencing.

Joe Murphy described the episode as a textbook case of Murphy’s law: he teaches the subject, his son works at sea, and then his son is taken captive.

Although worried, he said he trusted his son’s training and experience to help bring the confrontation to a successful conclusion. He expressed hope that everything would be resolved and that the episode would ultimately have a positive outcome.

CNN’s Jason Carroll and Tom Watkins also contributed to the report.

Despite being unarmed, the crew resisted and eventually regained control of the ship. They captured one pirate and forced the other three to leave the freighter.

Hoping to secure the release of Capt. Richard Phillips, the crew freed the captured pirate in a proposed hostage exchange. However, the exchange failed, and Phillips remained in the pirates’ custody. Because the pirates’ own boat had been scuttled, they took Phillips aboard the *Maersk Alabama*’s 28-foot lifeboat.

Meanwhile, the crew transmitted a distress signal, prompting an immediate response from the U.S. Navy, whose forces were nearly 200 miles away.
outputs.L4:
On April 8, 2009, four Somali pirates boarded the U.S.-flagged container ship *Maersk Alabama* in the Indian Ocean while it was carrying humanitarian aid and other cargo toward Mombasa, Kenya. The unarmed American crew had already sent a distress signal and attempted to prevent the takeover by increasing speed, making evasive maneuvers, and using fire hoses, but the pirates succeeded in reaching the deck.

Captain Richard Phillips instructed most of the crew to retreat to a secure area below deck. The sailors then shut down key systems, leaving the pirates unable to control the vessel effectively. Using their knowledge of the ship’s layout, crew members moved through darkened passageways, misled the attackers about their location, and eventually ambushed and captured one of them, Abduwali Muse. They hoped to exchange Muse for Phillips and end the hijacking.

The exchange broke down. Although the crew released Muse, the pirates refused to free Phillips. Instead, they forced the captain into one of the ship’s enclosed lifeboats and fled the *Maersk Alabama*, intending to take him to Somalia and demand a ransom.

The U.S. Navy responded immediately. The guided-missile destroyer USS *Bainbridge* intercepted the lifeboat, while additional American ships and Navy SEALs arrived to support the rescue effort. For several days, Navy personnel negotiated with the pirates as the lifeboat drifted in worsening conditions. On April 12, after commanders concluded that Phillips faced imminent danger, three Navy SEAL snipers simultaneously shot and killed the three pirates holding him. Muse, who was aboard the *Bainbridge* during negotiations, was taken into custody.

Phillips was rescued unharmed and reunited with his crew. Muse was transported to the United States, where he later pleaded guilty to charges connected with the hijacking and was sentenced to more than thirty-three years in federal prison.

## Buzzards Bay, Massachusetts

Buzzards Bay is a scenic coastal region in southeastern Massachusetts, separating Cape Cod from the mainland. Known for its sheltered waters, picturesque harbors, and small seaside communities, the bay has long played an important role in the area’s maritime history.

The Cape Cod Canal connects Buzzards Bay with Cape Cod Bay, creating a major route for commercial and recreational vessels. Along the shoreline, visitors can enjoy sailing, fishing, kayaking, swimming, and exploring beaches and nature preserves. The bay’s coves, marshes, and estuaries also provide valuable habitats for fish, shellfish, seabirds, and other wildlife.

Buzzards Bay is also the name of a village in the town of Bourne, located near the canal’s western entrance. With its coastal charm, working waterfronts, and easy access to Cape Cod, Buzzards Bay represents both the natural beauty and nautical character of Massachusetts.
